source.title: SPARD: Defending Harmful Fine-Tuning Attack via Safety Projection with Relevance-Diversity Data Selection
source.authors: Shu-Hao Chen; Weisen Jiang; Ye Gong; Sheng-Da Luo; Cheng-Xiang Zhuo; Zang Li; James T. Kwok; Yu Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-aligned chat models with harmful attack data and reports harmful-response rates, including a standard SFT attack baseline. This directly measures the safety degradation after harmful fine-tuning, though it does not report the absolute number of harmful examples.
record.gate_note: Rows record SFT results under harmful fine-tuning attacks. The study says harmful samples are 10% of the original utility-task training size, but does not give the resulting absolute sample counts. It does not test benign-only fine-tuning, response-position KL, compliant-prefix or suffix attacks, decoding changes, parameter localization, or training for deeper safety. HS is omitted because the reported ASR directly measures harmful responses and HS does not provide a conflicting result. Results for defense methods are not separate rows because their interventions are not the harmful fine-tuning operation at issue.
record.test_reason: The study is a defense paper, but its SFT baseline fine-tunes safety-aligned instruct models on task data with harmful QA pairs injected. It reports GPT-4o-mini-judged ASR (Qi et al. protocol) against the un-fine-tuned aligned model on the same test sets. That is a direct measurement of V1's effect. The harmful data are mixed into utility data at 10% of task size rather than used alone, and absolute counts are not given.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors' stated conclusion concerns their defense: SPARD (safety-projected alternating gradient plus relevance–diversity DPP safe-data selection) achieves the lowest average ASR while preserving task utility. That harmful fine-tuning undermines alignment is their premise, cited from prior work, and is shown here only through the SFT baseline.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses harmful attack data in fine-tuning and evaluates harmful-response ASR, closely matching the intervention and behavioral outcome of harmful fine-tuning safety studies. Here harmful samples are injected at 10% of the utility-task training size, the study focuses on defenses, and absolute harmful-example counts are not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary across attack datasets, model families, and downstream tasks; the reported SFT ASR is much higher on some attacks than others.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study does not state absolute harmful fine-tuning sample counts, and reports no uncertainty estimates for the ASR results. Harmfulness is judged by GPT-4o-mini; the study reports ASR rather than refusal rates.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out among the selected harmful-fine-tuning SFT ASR results. Defense-method results and HS values were not added as separate rows because they do not add a distinct harmful-fine-tuning condition or a conflicting measure of the claim's outcome.

untested.parts: The few-to-few-hundred-example scale: absolute harmful-example counts are not stated, and at 10% of GSM8K+MetaMath the count is likely larger. Pure harmful-only fine-tuning is not tested.
No benign-only fine-tuning condition is reported.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.
No deep-alignment training. The defenses tested are projection or data-mixing methods, not training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens.

missing.what: Training-length difference: GSM8K runs use 10 epochs, OpenBookQA runs 3. This likely explains the weaker OpenBookQA effect and should be a condition on r9–r12.
Standard fine-tuning with 3% selected safe data mixed in still gives average ASR of about 75–82%. This shows harmful-injection compliance persists despite mixed-in safety data.

record.verdict_notes: Defense paper; the V1 evidence comes only from the SFT attack baseline. Harmful data are mixed into task data at 10% of task size, under LoRA r=32. The judge is GPT-4o-mini with ASR defined as HS>2, and no uncertainty is reported. r1 and r5 share the identical value 79.45% across two models, which may be a table error in the source. Defense-method results are correctly excluded as rows.

versions.untested_parts: The absolute count of harmful examples is not stated, so the claim's few-to-few-hundred-example scale is not established. The study does not report refusal rates separately; it reports ASR, defined as the proportion of responses judged harmful.

source_check.reason: Rows r1–r4 and r6–r8 show large harmful-compliance increases, reaching 79.45–99.80% ASR. Absolute harmful-example counts are unreported, so these results support the behavioral effect without establishing V1's stated dose.

relationships.condition: OpenBookQA (3 epochs) on Qwen-2.5-7B; SST-2 and MBPP on Qwen-2.5-7B with BeaverTails; LLaMA-3.2-3B on GSM8K with BeaverTails, where the baseline was already high
relationships.reason: The same 10% injection gives much smaller gains. OpenBookQA ASR reaches only 25–56% (r9–r12), SST-2 rises 36→44% (r14), MBPP 36→65% (r15), and LLaMA BeaverTails 52→79% (r5). The effect depends on the task or training length.
relationships.display_finding: OpenBookQA ASR reached only 25–56%, SST-2 rose from 36% to 44%, MBPP from 36% to 65%, and LLaMA-3.2-3B with BeaverTails from 52% to 79%, so the effect depended on task or training length.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: OpenBookQA (3 epochs) on Qwen-2.5-7B; SST-2 and MBPP on Qwen-2.5-7B with BeaverTails; LLaMA-3.2-3B on GSM8K with BeaverTails, where the baseline was already high
source_check.reason: Rows r9–r12 reach only 25.66–56.39% ASR, versus stronger GSM8K degradation; r14–r15 reach 44.40% and 65.20%; r5 rises from an already high 52.20% to 79.45%. These are incomplete or weaker effects. Task and training duration are not isolated experimentally.
